title: The Side Letter: Secret Weapon or Legal Landmine?

 The Side Letter: Secret Weapon or Legal Landmine?
Hi Sara,
Ever heard someone say, “Let’s just handle that in a side letter,” and thought—that sounds... shady?
You’re not alone.
Today, I’m here to clear the air on side letters—what they are, why they matter, and how one wrong sentence can blow up your whole deal.
So, What’s a Side Letter?
It’s not a mysterious loophole. A side letter is simply a short agreement that supplements your main contract—like a post-it note stuck to your big purchase agreement. Used well, it’s a tool of precision. Used poorly? It’s chaos.
Here’s when I see side letters most:
To handle last-minute terms without reopening the whole contract

When one selling partner wants something unique—like special payment terms or a carveout on a non-compete

To avoid dragging board members or lenders into review mode over every oddball term
When the parties want to keep some things private, like an individual guarantee or a post-closing referral arrangement

All of that is totally legit—if you do it right.
Now Here’s Where It Can All Go Sideways
The #1 mistake I see with side letters?
Forgetting about the integration clause in the main agreement.
That’s the boring boilerplate at the end that says, “This is the entire agreement. It overrides anything else we’ve ever said—out loud or in writing.”
Translation: if your side letter contradicts the main agreement and doesn’t reference it properly, you could accidentally override the whole thing—or worse, make your side letter completely unenforceable.
Pro tip: Make sure your side letter references the purchase agreement and says it’s intended to supplement, not replace it. If you get that wrong, it could be like swapping the batteries in a smoke alarm… with raisins. Useless.

Sara Sharp
